citation.title: Average treatment effects in the presence of unknown interference

standing_assumptions: [Setting: Section 3.1, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] Consider a sample of $n$ units indexed by the set $\mathbf{U} = \{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$. An experimenter intervenes on the world in ways that potentially affect the units. The intervention is described by a $n$-dimensional binary vector $\mathbf{z} = (z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_n) \in \{0, 1\}^n$. For short, we refer to $z_i$ as unit $i$'s treatment. Each unit has a function $y_i : \{0, 1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ denoting the observed outcome for the unit under a specific and potentially counterfactual intervention. In particular, $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ is the response of $i$ when the intervention is $\mathbf{z}$. We refer to the elements of the image of this function as potential outcomes. Let $\mathbf{z}_{-i} = (z_1, \ldots, z_{i-1}, z_{i+1}, \ldots, z_n)$ denote the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\mathbf{z}$. The potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf{z})$ can then be written as $y_i(z_i; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. Throughout the paper, we assume that the potential outcomes are well-defined. The experimenter sets $\mathbf{z}$ according to a random vector $\mathbf{Z} = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$. The probability distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ is the design of the experiment. The design is the sole source of randomness we will consider. Let $Y_i$ denote the observed outcome of unit $i$: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z})$. As above, $\mathbf{Z}_{-i}$ denotes $\mathbf{Z}$ without its $i$th element, so $Y_i = y_i(Z_i; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})$. [No interference: Section 3.2, p. 676 (PDF p. 4)] It is conventional to assume that the potential outcomes are restricted so a unit's outcome is only affected by its own treatment. That is, for any two assignments $\mathbf{z}$ and $\mathbf{z}'$, if the treatment of a given unit is the same for both assignments, then the outcome for that unit is also the same. This no-interference assumption admits a definition of the treatment effect $\tau_i$ for unit $i$: $\tau_i = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$, where $\mathbf{z}_{-i}$ is any element of $\{0, 1\}^{n-1}$. [Definitions 1 to 3: p. 677 (PDF p. 5)] DEFINITION 1. Under no interference, the average treatment effect (ATE) is the average unit-level treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i$. The assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect is $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i}) = y_i(1; \mathbf{z}_{-i}) - y_i(0; \mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 2. An assignment-conditional average treatment effect is the average of the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effects under a given assignment: $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$. DEFINITION 3. The expected average treatment effect (EATE) is the expected assignment-conditional average treatment effect: $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathrm{E}[\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{Z})]$, where the expectation is taken over the distribution of $\mathbf{Z}$ given by the experimental design. [Definition 4: p. 678 (PDF p. 6)] DEFINITION 4. The average distributional shift effect (ADSE) is the average difference between the conditional expected outcomes for the two treatment conditions: $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y_i \mid Z_i = 0]\right)$. [Interference indicator: Section 4, p. 680 (PDF p. 8)] We say that unit $i$ interferes with unit $j$ if changing $i$'s treatment changes $j$'s outcome under at least one treatment assignment. We also say that a unit interferes with itself even if its own treatment does not affect its outcome. The indicator $I_{ij}$ denotes such interference: $I_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } y_j(\mathbf{z}) \ne y_j(\mathbf{z}') \text{ for some } \mathbf{z}, \mathbf{z}' \in \{0, 1\}^n \text{ such that } \mathbf{z}_{-i} = \mathbf{z}'_{-i}, \\ 1 & \text{if } i = j, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Definition 5 (Interference dependence): p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ where $d_{ij} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } I_{\ell i} I_{\ell j} = 1 \text{ for some } \ell \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ The sum $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} d_{ij}$ gives the number of interference dependencies for unit $i$. [Interference counts: p. 681 (PDF p. 9)] $c_i = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_{ij}$ and $C_p = \left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} c_i^p\right]^{1/p}$. We write $C_\infty$ for the limit of $C_p$ as $p \to \infty$, which is the maximum $c_i$ over $\mathbf{U}$. [Asymptotic regime: Section 5, pp. 681–682 (PDF pp. 9–10)] We consider an arbitrary sequence of samples indexed by their sample size. The samples are not assumed to be drawn from some larger population or otherwise randomly generated. All quantities describing the samples, such as the potential outcomes and experimental designs, have their own sequences also indexed by $n$. But we leave the indexing implicit as no confusion arises. [Definition 6: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] The Horvitz–Thompson (HT) and Hájek (HÁ) estimators are $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i}$ and $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i Y_i}{p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{Z_i}{p_i}\right) - \left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(1 - Z_i)Y_i}{1 - p_i} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1 - Z_i}{1 - p_i}\right)$, where $p_i = \Pr(Z_i = 1)$ is the marginal treatment probability for unit $i$. [Assumption 1: p. 682 (PDF p. 10)] We assume throughout the remainder of the paper that the experimental design and potential outcomes are sufficiently well behaved, as formalized in the following assumption. ASSUMPTION 1 (Regularity conditions). There exist constants $k < \infty$, $q \ge 2$ and $s \ge 1$ such that for all $i \in \mathbf{U}$ in the sequence of samples: A (Probabilistic assignment). $k^{-1} \le \Pr(Z_i = 1) \le 1 - k^{-1}$, B (Outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|Y_i|^q] \le k^q$, C (Potential outcome moments). $\mathrm{E}[|y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})|^s] \le k^s$ for $z \in \{0, 1\}$. [Assumption 2: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] ASSUMPTION 2 (Restricted interference). $d_{\mathrm{AVG}} = o(n)$. [Bernoulli design: p. 683 (PDF p. 11)] We call this a Bernoulli randomization design, and it satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i^{z_i}(1 - p_i)^{1 - z_i}$ for some set of assignment probabilities $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ bounded away from zero and one. [Complete randomization: p. 684 (PDF p. 12)] $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} \binom{n}{m}^{-1} & \text{if } \sum_{i=1}^{n} z_i = m, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases}$ where $m = \lfloor pn \rfloor$ for some fixed $p$ strictly between zero and one. We call the design complete randomization. [Paired randomization: p. 685 (PDF p. 13)] It is implicit that the sample size is even so that all units are paired. Let $\rho : \mathbf{U} \to \mathbf{U}$ describe a pairing so that $\rho(i) = j$ indicates that units $i$ and $j$ are paired. The pairing is symmetric, so the self-composition of $\rho$ is the identity function. The paired randomization design then satisfies $\Pr(\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{z}) = \begin{cases} 2^{-n/2} & \text{if } z_i \ne z_{\rho(i)} \text{ for all } i \in \mathbf{U}, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$ [Notation the paper uses without defining] The paper does not define $\mathcal{O}_p$, $o_p$, 'consistent' or 'root-$n$ consistent'. The proof of Lemma A5 (Supplement A, p. 4) uses $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$ in the sense that for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there are a constant $\kappa$ and an $N$ such that $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$. 'Consistent for' an estimand means that the difference between the estimator and the estimand (both sequences in $n$) converges in probability to zero; 'root-$n$ consistent' means that this difference is $\mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5})$. Supplement A is the separate file 'Supplement A: Proofs' (41 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPA) and Supplement B is 'Supplement B: Simulation study' (21 pp., DOI 10.1214/20-AOS1973SUPPB); their page numbers are their own printed page numbers, which equal their PDF page numbers. In the main article the printed page number is the PDF page number plus 672.

canonical_claim.location: p. 688 (PDF p. 16); proof in Supplement A, Section 9, pp. 18–22
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 5. Under restricted interference, design mixing and design separation (Assumptions 2, 5 and 6), the HT and HÁ estimators are consistent for EATE and converge at the following rates: $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-0.5}\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}^{0.5} + n^{-1}\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}})$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-0.5}\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}^{0.5} + n^{-1}\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}})$. [Standing hypothesis: Assumption 1; the design is arbitrary; $q$ and $s$ in Definition 9 are the exponents of Assumption 1.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: In the standing assumptions: the setting, $y_i$, $\mathbf{Z}$, $Y_i$ (p. 676); $\tau_i(\mathbf{z}_{-i})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ATE}}(\mathbf{z})$, $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}$ (p. 677); $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ (p. 678); $I_{ij}$ (p. 680); $d_{ij}$, $d_i$, $d_{\mathrm{AVG}}$, $c_i$, $C_p$, $C_\infty$ (p. 681); $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}}$, $p_i$, Assumption 1 (p. 682); Assumption 2 and the Bernoulli design (p. 683); complete randomization (p. 684); paired randomization (p. 685); the senses of $\mathcal{O}_p$ and 'consistent'. [Definition A1 and Corollary A1: Supplement A, p. 2] DEFINITION A1. $\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i})]$, $\breve\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathrm{E}[y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) \mid Z_i = z]$, $\hat\mu_z = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]Y_i}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$, $\hat n_z = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\mathbb{1}[Z_i = z]}{\Pr(Z_i = z)}$. COROLLARY A1. $\tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = \mu_1 - \mu_0$, $\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \breve\mu_1 - \breve\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} = \hat\mu_1 - \hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} = \frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = (\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1) - (\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0)$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{H\acute{A}}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} = \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_1}\hat\mu_1 - \breve\mu_1\right) - \left(\frac{n}{\hat n_0}\hat\mu_0 - \breve\mu_0\right)$. [Assignment vectors affecting a unit: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i = (I_{1i}Z_1, I_{2i}Z_2, \ldots, I_{ni}Z_n)$. The vector is defined so that its $j$th element is $Z_j$ if unit $j$ is interfering with $i$, and zero otherwise. Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i}$ be the $(n-1)$-dimensional vector constructed by deleting the $i$th element from $\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i$. The definitions have the following convenient properties: $Y_i = y_i(\mathbf{Z}) = y_i(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i)$ and $y_i(z; \mathbf{Z}_{-i}) = y_i(z; \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})$. [Alpha-mixing coefficient: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For two random variables $X$ and $Y$ defined on the same probability space, let $\alpha(X, Y) = \sup_{x \in \sigma(X),\, y \in \sigma(Y)} \left|\Pr(x \cap y) - \Pr(x)\Pr(y)\right|$, where $\sigma(X)$ and $\sigma(Y)$ denote the sub-sigma-algebras generated by the random variables. The coefficient $\alpha(X, Y)$ is zero if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent. The maximum is $\alpha(X, Y) = 1/4$. [Definition 9 (External and internal average mixing coefficients): p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] For the maximum values of $q$ and $s$ such that Assumptions 1B and 1C hold, let $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}(1 - d_{ij})\left[\alpha(\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_j)\right]^{\frac{q-2}{q}}$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\alpha(Z_i, \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}_{-i})\right]^{\frac{s-1}{s}}$, where $0^0$ is defined as zero to accommodate the cases $q = 2$ and $s = 1$. [Assumptions 5 and 6: p. 687 (PDF p. 15)] ASSUMPTION 5 (Design mixing). $\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}} = o(n)$. ASSUMPTION 6 (Design separation). $\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}} = o(n)$. [Lemmas used to pass from exact moments to rates: Supplement A] LEMMA A1 (p. 3). $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_z] = \breve\mu_z$. LEMMA A2 (p. 3). $\mathrm{E}[\hat n_z] = n$. LEMMA A5 (p. 4). If the rate of convergence in the $L_2$-norm for a sequence of random variables is govern by a sequence $(a_n)$, then the rate of convergence in probability is govern by $(a_n)$ [that is, in the notation of its proof, $\sqrt{\mathrm{E}[(X_n - x_n)^2]} = \mathcal{O}(a_n)$ implies $X_n - x_n = \mathcal{O}_p(a_n)$; the proof is Markov's inequality, $\Pr(|X_n - x_n| \ge \kappa a_n) \le \mathrm{E}[(X_n - x_n)^2]/(\kappa^2 a_n^2)$]. LEMMA A6 (p. 4). If $\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = o_p(1)$ and $\hat n_z/n - 1 = o_p(1)$, then: $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \mathcal{O}_p\left((\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z) + (\hat n_z/n - 1)\right)$ [read with the magnitudes of the two errors, clarity note P009-E011; its proof rests on the exact identity $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \frac{\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z}{\hat n_z/n} - \frac{(\hat n_z/n - 1)\breve\mu_z}{\hat n_z/n}$ and on $|\breve\mu_z| \le k^2$].
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Supplement A, pp. 18–22] For each fixed $n$, for an arbitrary design and Assumption 1 with constant $k$: (a) LEMMA A20 (p. 18). Under arbitrary experimental designs, $|\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}}| \le 6k^2 n^{-1}\alpha_{\mathrm{INT}}$. (b) $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}} = (\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}} - \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}) + (\tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}} - \tau_{\mathrm{EATE}})$ and the same for the Hájek estimator (p. 22). (c) The finite lemmas of Proposition 6 for the first term.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H5; it held up, with caveats about proof steps that leave the statement unchanged (P009-E009 and P009-E010, through Proposition 6). The paper proves it from Proposition 6 and Lemma A20. The phrase 'the maximum values of $q$ and $s$' in Definition 9 needs the convention that an infinite exponent is admitted when outcomes are bounded (clarity note P009-E006). The proof of Lemma A20 is a truncation argument that the paper derives itself; it was followed by both readers.

canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: [Supplement A, pp. 3 and 22–24] For each fixed $n$, for an arbitrary design and Assumption 1 with constant $k$ and exponent $q$: (a) $\mathrm{E}[\hat\mu_z] = \breve\mu_z$ (Lemma A1), so $\mathrm{E}[\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}] = \tau_{\mathrm{ADSE}}$ for any design, and $\mathrm{E}[\hat n_z] = n$ (Lemma A2). (b) LEMMA A21 (p. 22). Let $X$ and $Y$ be two arbitrary random variables defined on the same probability space such that $\mathrm{E}[|X|^a] \le c^a$ and $\mathrm{E}[|Y|^b] \le c^b$ for some constants $a$, $b$ and $c$ where $a^{-1} + b^{-1} \le 1$, we then have: $|\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)| \le 10[\alpha(X, Y)]^{1 - 1/a - 1/b}\mathrm{E}[|X|^a]^{1/a}\mathrm{E}[|Y|^b]^{1/b}$. (c) From the proof of Lemma A22 (pp. 22–23): $\mathrm{Var}(\hat\mu_z) \le k^4 n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}} + 10k^4 n^{-1}\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}$. (d) From the proof of Lemma A23 (p. 23): $\mathrm{Var}(\hat n_z/n) \le k^2 n^{-1}d_{\mathrm{AVG}} + k^2 n^{-1}\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}$. (e) Corollary A1 and the identity of Lemma A6. The chains leading to (c) and (d), with their first steps corrected, are in the corrected-statement targets for P009-E009 and P009-E010.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P009-H5; it held up, with the caveat that the first inequality in the proofs of Lemmas A22 and A23 is false as printed (P009-E009) and that one display of the proof of Lemma A23 drops the diagonal (P009-E010); the final bounds (c) and (d) are unchanged. Lemma A22 (p. 22): under arbitrary experimental designs, $\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z = \mathcal{O}_p(n^{-0.5}d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{0.5} + n^{-0.5}\alpha_{\mathrm{EXT}}^{0.5})$; Lemma A23 (p. 23): under arbitrary experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 2 and 5, the same rate for $\frac{n}{\hat n_z}\hat\mu_z - \breve\mu_z$. Lemma A21 is taken from Davydov (1970); whether the attribution is exact is recorded as undetermined (P009-N004), and a formalizer may need it as a named assumption.

canonical_claim.location: Proposition 7: p. 690 (PDF p. 18); equation (1): p. 689 (PDF p. 17); proof and Corollary A5 in Supplement A, Section 11, pp. 24–30
canonical_claim.statement: PROPOSITION 7. Under a Bernoulli design and Assumption 1 with $q \ge 4$, $n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}^{-1}\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})\right] \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \frac{\tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}}}{d_{\mathrm{AVG}}} - B_1 - B_2$, where $B_1 = \frac{1}{n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j \ne i}\left(\breve\xi_{ij}\breve\xi_{ji} + 2\breve Y_j[\xi_{ij}(1) - \xi_{ij}(0)]\right)$, $B_2 = \frac{1}{n d_{\mathrm{AVG}}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j \ne i}\sum_{a=0}^{1}\sum_{b=0}^{1}(-1)^{a+b}\mathrm{Cov}(Y_i, Y_j \mid Z_i = a, Z_j = b)$. [Equation (1), p. 689] In particular, with a Bernoulli design under no interference, $n\left[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{BER}}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}}) - \mathrm{Var}(\hat\tau_{\mathrm{HT}})\right] \overset{p}{\longrightarrow} \tau_{\mathrm{MSQ}} \ge 0$. [Supplement A, p. 30] COROLLARY A5.
